pass_a_gloss: For example, when it is said in the Epistle to the Galatians that those who are of the works of the law are under a curse, for it is written: Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things written in the book of the law to do them; it is clear that the law according to the letter is proclaimed by Moses, the prescriptive part being what must be done, the prohibitive part being what must not be done to those under it; the same is also shown in the same epistle and in the statement that the law was added because of transgressions until the seed should come to whom the promise was made, ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator; and in the statement that the law has become our guardian until Christ, that we might be justified by faith; but after faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian; for all are sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus; and the history written by Moses is signified as coming from the voice of the law, as from the same epistle it is possible to take: Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman; but he who was of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, and he who was of the free woman through promise; and I also know the psalms called law, as it is evident from that the word in their law might be fulfilled: I ate them gladly; but also the prophecy of Isaiah is called law by the apostle, saying: It is written in the law: With men of other tongues and other lips will I speak to this people; and even then they will not hear me, says the Lord; for I have found the things equal to this saying in the translation of Aquila; it is said that the law and the more mystical and divine interpretation of the law, as in we know that the law is spiritual; but besides all these, the law is said to be that which is implanted in the mind by common notions and, as the Scripture says, written on the heart, word, prescriptive of what must be done, prohibitive of what must not be done; and this is also shown in that when Gentiles who do not have the law by nature do the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves, in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness and their thoughts accusing or else excusing them; for the law written in the hearts and in the Gentiles doing by nature the things of the law is not other than that which is implanted by nature in the common notions written on the ruling part of us, and more clearly with the filling out of the word being done today; this meaning of the law was in the sin not being imputed when there was no law; and in the sin not being known except through law; for before the law of Moses sin was imputed to Cain and to those in the flood, and still also to the Sodomites and countless others; and many knew sin before the law of Moses; and do not wonder if two meanings of the one name law are taken in the same place, for we will find this usage also in other writings, as when you do not say that four-monthly is it and the summer comes? Lift up your eyes and see the land that it is white already for harvest; for the harvest is named twice, according to the former referring to the bodily, according to the latter referring to the spiritual; and you will find the same also in the case of the man born blind who was healed, to whom He said, having become bodily: I judge that I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind; thus now, apart from the law of nature, the righteousness of God has been revealed, witnessed by the law of Moses and the prophets; but we could say to those still hesitating to accept the twofold meaning of the law, that if the same law is received both now and apart from the law the righteousness of God has been revealed, and in the witnessed by the law and the prophets; if apart from the law it has been revealed, it is not witnessed by the law; if witnessed by the law, it is not apart from the law; to the righteousness of God being revealed through Jesus Christ, the law of nature does not witness at all, for it is weaker than it; but the law of Moses, not the letter but the spirit, and those analogous to the spirit of the law, the prophets, and the spiritual word in them; therefore let the one reading the divine writing carefully observe that the writings do not always use the same words for the same things; but they do this, sometimes
pass_b_english: For instance, when the Epistle to the Galatians declares that those who rely on works of the law stand under a curse, quoting Scripture: 'Cursed is everyone who fails to uphold every command written in the book of the law,' it becomes evident that the law as given by Moses comprises both prescriptive demands—what must be done—and prohibitive warnings—what must be avoided—by those subject to it. This dual character is reinforced elsewhere in the same letter, where we learn the law was added due to transgressions, serving as a temporary guardian until the promised offspring arrived, instituted through angelic mediation. Likewise, the law functioned as our custodian until Christ, so that justification might come through faith; but once faith emerged, we are no longer under such supervision, for all who believe in Christ Jesus are sons of God. The historical narrative authored by Moses is thus revealed as an expression of the law’s voice, as when the Galatian epistle challenges: 'Tell me, you who wish to be under the law, do you not hear what it says?' For it is recorded that Abraham had two sons—one by the slave woman, born according to the flesh, and one by the free woman, born through promise. I also recognize the Psalms as bearing the name 'law,' since their fulfillment is seen in the words: 'I ate them with gladness.' Furthermore, the prophecy of Isaiah is termed 'law' by the apostle, citing: 'It is written in the law: I will speak to this people with strangers’ tongues and foreign lips; yet even then they will not listen,' declares the Lord—a sentiment I find echoed in Aquila’s translation. Moreover, the law is understood not only in its external form but also in its deeper, spiritual dimension, as we affirm: 'The law is spiritual.' Beyond this, the law is described as that which is inwardly implanted by common notions and, as Scripture affirms, 'written on the heart'—a word that prescribes duty and forbids transgression. This is further confirmed when Gentiles, who lack the law by nature, nevertheless perform its requirements; they become a law to themselves, demonstrating the work of the law inscribed in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness, their thoughts either accusing or excusing them. For the law written in the hearts and practiced by Gentiles through nature is none other than that which is innately engraved in the rational faculty by common conception, now being more fully realized in our time. This understanding of the law was operative even before sin was imputed in the absence of law, or known only through law; for prior to the Mosaic law, sin was charged to Cain and to those in the flood, and still to the Sodomites and countless others, and many had knowledge of sin long before Moses. There is no need to be surprised when a single term like 'law' carries two meanings in the same context, for this pattern appears elsewhere—for example, when you do not say: 'Is it four-monthly, and does summer come?' Lift your eyes and behold the land: it is already white for harvest. Indeed, the harvest is named twice—first referring to the physical gathering, then to the spiritual ingathering. The same duality appears in the man born blind who was healed; when addressed in bodily terms, He declared: 'I have come into this world so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.' Thus, apart from the law of nature, God’s righteousness has been unveiled, attested by the law of Moses and the prophets. Yet to those still hesitant to accept the twofold sense of 'law,' we might say: if the same law is received both now and apart from it, and God’s righteousness is revealed in both cases, witnessed by law and prophets, then if it is revealed apart from the law, it is not witnessed by the law; if witnessed by the law, it is not separate from it. But concerning the righteousness of God revealed in Jesus Christ, the law of nature bears no testimony at all, for it is inferior to it; whereas the Mosaic law—not in its letter but in its spirit, along with those who embody its spirit—the prophets, and the indwelling spiritual word—do bear witness. Therefore, let the attentive reader of sacred Scripture observe that writings do not always employ identical terms for identical realities, yet they do so intentionally, sometimes…
